opening: Why does an LLM application need context beyond what the model learned during training? Describe different ways to provide context and give examples of when they would be useful.
closing: That's the end of today's review. Nice work thinking these through. You can press End conversation whenever you're ready.
note: Ask the three questions in order. Require the learner’s own explanation, not keywords. Hints reduce the reasoning task: focus on one part, identify what it does, then connect it to the rest. Choose a hint for the actual gap rather than mechanically reading all hints. Never supply an answer or a worked example. After five completed unsuccessful hint-and-response exchanges on a question, move on without implying mastery.

questions.objective: Distinguish model parameters from situated information and choose suitable context sources.
questions.question: Why does an LLM application need context beyond what the model learned during training? Describe different ways to provide context and give examples of when they would be useful.
questions.goodEnough: Explains that training does not automatically supply current, private, user-specific or task-specific information and that adding context does not update weights. Describes several complementary context methods with concrete uses, distinguishing direct documents, retrieved evidence, saved learner history and live tool results; may also discuss structured knowledge, current task state or clarification. Require the learner to explain the relevant roles, relationships or reasons in their own words; a list of keywords, repetition of the question or unsupported assertions alone is insufficient. Accept concise explanations and equivalent terminology.
lookFor: direct context: attach a small set of lecture notes
RAG: select relevant passages from a larger or changing collection
structured knowledge / OKF: organize linked concepts for navigation or retrieval
memory: select and recall previous mistakes or preferences
tools / APIs: obtain current deadlines or live availability
current task state and asking the user: supply the draft, selected passage or missing goal
context changes model input, not model parameters; methods can be combined
hints: Focus on one request from a user. What information would someone need to answer it?
Which of that information depends on this particular user or on when they ask?
Choose one piece the model might be missing. Where could the application get it?
How would that information reach the model before it answers?
Choose a second kind of missing information. Would you get it the same way? Explain your choice.
misconceptions: adding documents to a prompt retrains the model
the model automatically knows private records or current facts
saved memory is useful even when it is never brought into context
RAG, memory and tools are mutually exclusive

questions.objective: Explain the preparation and question-time pipelines and distinguish retrieval from generation failures.
questions.question: Explain each step of a RAG pipeline in your own words, from document preparation to answer generation.
questions.goodEnough: Describes preparing source documents, splitting them into meaningful chunks while retaining metadata, embedding chunks and storing vectors linked to text in an index. At question time, embeds the query in a compatible space, retrieves and filters relevant candidates (optionally reranking), assembles selected evidence within the context budget, and generates an evidence-grounded answer with sources or acknowledges missing or conflicting evidence. Require the learner to explain the relevant roles, relationships or reasons in their own words; a list of keywords, repetition of the question or unsupported assertions alone is insufficient. Accept concise explanations and equivalent terminology.
lookFor: prepare documents and retain source, date/version and access metadata
split into meaningful chunks with a trade-off between lost context and diluted relevance
embed chunks and store vectors linked to passages in a search index
embed the query using a compatible encoder and retrieve candidate passages
filter by permission/version; optionally use keyword search or reranking
assemble selected text as context within the input budget
generate a supported answer, identify sources and acknowledge conflicts or insufficient evidence
hints: Start with a collection of long documents. What would make it easier to find just the part needed for a question?
Once you have smaller passages, what would you need to keep with them so you can find and use them later?
Now a question arrives. How could the system decide which stored passages to look at?
After choosing passages, what should be passed to the model that will write the answer?
Look back at your steps. What does each one provide that the next step needs?
misconceptions: RAG trains the generator on each retrieved document
the index stores only vectors without a link to source text
retrieval and generation are the same step
all retrieved documents should always be included

questions.objective: Explain semantic retrieval without treating similarity as truth or answer relevance.
questions.question: What is a vector embedding, and how does it help a RAG system find relevant information? Explain why the most similar passage may not always answer the user’s question.
questions.goodEnough: Describes an embedding as an ordered numerical vector representing text, and explains comparing query and passage vectors in a compatible space, for example using cosine similarity, to retrieve related meanings despite different wording. Explains with a concrete example why related topic is not sufficient evidence: a passage may omit the requested fact, be outdated, refer to a different entity or contain opposite claims. Recognizes that top-k can return neighbors even when no passage answers the question. Require the learner to explain the relevant roles, relationships or reasons in their own words; a list of keywords, repetition of the question or unsupported assertions alone is insufficient. Accept concise explanations and equivalent terminology.
lookFor: embedding model maps text to an ordered list of numbers
query and document vectors must share a compatible embedding space
similarity search can match borrow a camera with equipment reservation
cosine similarity compares directions, not probability of truth
related passages may disagree, omit the answer or have the wrong date/product
top-k still returns candidates when no relevant answer exists; inspect evidence and exact details
hints: Start with the output of an embedding model. What kind of thing does it produce from text?
If you have that output for a question and for a passage, what could you compare?
What is the search trying to find by making that comparison?
Focus on the information the user asked for. What would you need to see inside the passage before using it to answer?
What might be missing from a passage even when it is closely related to the question?
misconceptions: an embedding is a stored natural-language answer
a similarity of 0.9 means a 90 percent chance of truth
the nearest passage necessarily contains the answer
arbitrary embedding models produce directly comparable vectors
